title: Singapore's hawker centres: history, recognition and the succession problem

sources.title: Hawker Culture Is Singapore’s First Inscription On UNESCO’s Representative List Of The Intangible Cultural Heritage Of Humanity
How Singapore street food got recognized as a UNESCO treasure
The History and Evolution of Singapore's Hawker Culture
Singapore offers the world’s cheapest Michelin-star meal

facts.text: Hawkers once sold food from carts and baskets on the streets; crowding and poor hygiene led the government to move them into purpose-built centres.
Most hawker centres were built in the 1970s and 1980s to resettle street hawkers.
Hawker centres bring together people of Chinese, Malay, Indian and other backgrounds, who often share tables.
Typical dishes include Hainanese chicken rice, Malay satay, Indian rojak and laksa.
A meal at a hawker centre costs only a few Singapore dollars.
In July 2016 two hawker stalls each received one Michelin star, making a soy sauce chicken rice dish the cheapest Michelin-starred meal in the world.
On 16 December 2020 hawker culture in Singapore was added to UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Hawkers work very long hours, some starting around 3 a.m.
Many hawkers are retiring, and few younger people, including their own children, want to take over, so some recipes risk disappearing.
Singapore encourages veteran hawkers to pass their recipes and skills to younger family members or apprentices.
